blocks.text: Introduction

The Greek mathematicians Apollonius (260-200 B.C.) and Pappus (early fourth century A.D.) made significant contributions to the study of conic sections using Euclidean geometry. Here, we will employ the methods of analytic geometry to investigate their properties.
The theory of conics has important applications in various fields, including space mechanics, oceanography, and many other branches of science and technology.

Consider a circle, with its centre C, draw a line RS passes through c and perpendicular to the circle's plane. Choose a fixed point A on this line. Now, from A, draw every possible straight line that touches some point on the circle. These lines together form a surface known as a right circular cone. Each of these straight lines is called a generator (or a ruling) of the cone. The complete surface has two separate parts, called nappes, which meet only at point A. This meeting point is the vertex of the cone and the original line RS is the axis of come.
book_errors: draw a line RS passes through c

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book prints "draw a line RS passes through c". It should read: "draw a line RS that passes through C and is perpendicular to the circle's plane" (C, the centre, is a capital letter).
The book prints "the axis of come". It should read: "the axis of the cone".
When you slice this cone with a plane, the intersection curve is called a conic section (or simply conics).

There are also special cases called degenerate conics. These happen when the slicing plane passes through the vertex A. Instead of getting a nice curve, the intersection might be just a single point, a single straight line, or a pair of intersecting lines.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Picture two ice-cream cones joined tip to tip, one upright and one upside down, and imagine them extended without end. That double cone is the solid in the book's description: A is the common tip (vertex), RS is the centre line (axis), and each slanting straight line through A along the surface is a generator. The upper and lower cones are the two nappes.
Now cut this double cone with a flat sheet (a plane). The edge of the cut is a curve. Which curve you get depends only on how the plane is tilted compared with the axis and with the generators. Figure 6.1 below shows each cut from the side, so the plane appears as a straight line and the curve appears as the thick green segment where the plane is inside the cone.

blocks.alt: Four double cones side by side: each light-blue double cone has a dotted axis RS through the vertex A, with C marked at the centre of the top rim. (a) Circle: a horizontal grey plane cuts the lower nappe in a circle; (b) Ellipse: a slightly tilted plane cuts it in an ellipse; (c) Parabola: a plane parallel to a generator cuts it in a parabola; (d) Hyperbola: a vertical plane cuts both nappes in the two branches of a hyperbola.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.1(a)-(d): plane sections of a double cone, shown in side view (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.1)

blocks.text: Depending on the angle and position of the plane, you can get a circle, an ellipse, a parabola, or a hyperbola.
When this cone is intersected by a plane, different curves are obtained depending on the angle and position of the cutting plane:

items: If the cutting plane is perpendicular to the axis, the section is a circle, see Figure 6.1(a).
If the plane is slightly inclined and cuts only one nappe, the resulting curve is an ellipse, see Figure 6.1(b).
If the plane is parallel to a generator and cuts only one nappe, the curve is a parabola, see Figure 6.1(c).
If the plane is parallel to the axis and cuts both nappes, the curve is a hyperbola, see Figure 6.1(d).

blocks.text: We will being our study with the circle. Other conic sections will be discussed in subsequent section.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
One way to remember the four cases is to compare the tilt of the plane with the tilt of a generator:
1. Plane perpendicular to the axis (no tilt): circle.
2. Plane tilted, but less steep than a generator: it still cuts right across one nappe and the curve closes: ellipse.
3. Plane exactly as steep as a generator (parallel to it): the curve never closes, it runs off along the nappe: parabola.
4. Plane steeper than a generator (for example parallel to the axis): it cuts both nappes: hyperbola, which has two separate branches.
All four curves will turn out to have second-degree equations in \(x\) and \(y\). In this unit we study each one with coordinates: circle (6.1, 6.2), parabola (6.3), ellipse (6.4) and hyperbola (6.5).
Circle
A circle is the set of all points in a plane that are at a fixed distance from a given fixed point. The fixed point is called the centre, and the fixed distance is called the radius of the circle.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
This definition is exactly what a compass does: the needle stays at one fixed point (the centre) and the pencil stays at one fixed distance (the radius) from it. Every point the pencil touches is on the circle, and no other point is.
To turn this sentence into an equation, we only need one tool from Class XI: the distance formula. The distance between \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) and \((x_{2}, y_{2})\) is
\[d = \sqrt{(x_{2} - x_{1})^{2} + (y_{2} - y_{1})^{2}}\]
Theorem 1: Equation of a circle with centre at the point \((h, k)\) and radius \(r\) is \((x - h)^{2} + (y - k)^{2} = r^{2}\).

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel, magenta X- and Y-axes from the origin O (marked with a dot), a cyan circle with centre C(h, k) and a black radius r to the point P(x, y) on the circle.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.2: circle with centre C(h, k) and radius r (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.2)

blocks.text:
Proof: Let \(C(h, k)\) be the centre of the circle and \(r\) be its radius. Let \(P(x, y)\) be any point on the circle. Then by definition, the distance \(|\overline{CP}|\) is equal to \(r\). Using the distance formula between the points \(P(x, y)\) and \(C(h, k)\), we obtain
\[\sqrt{(x - h)^{2} + (y - k)^{2}} = r\]
Squaring both sides gives
\[(x - h)^{2} + (y - k)^{2} = r^{2} \quad \text{...(1)}\]
which is the required equation of the circle.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is it safe to square both sides? Both sides are lengths, so both are non-negative; squaring two non-negative numbers keeps an equality true in both directions. So every point satisfying (1) is at distance \(r\) from \(C\), and every point at distance \(r\) satisfies (1).
Reading the equation: the numbers subtracted from \(x\) and \(y\) are the coordinates of the centre, and the right-hand side is the square of the radius. For example, \((x - 3)^{2} + (y + 4)^{2} = 25\) is \((x - 3)^{2} + (y - (-4))^{2} = 5^{2}\): centre \((3, -4)\), radius 5.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text:
(i) Equation (1) is known as the standard form of the equation of a circle.
(ii) If \(r = 0\), equation (1) reduces to \((x - h)^{2} + (y - k)^{2} = 0\). This represents a point circle centered at \((h, k)\).
(iii) If \((h, k) = (0, 0)\), then equation (1) reduces to \(x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2}\). This equation represents a circle whose centre is at origin.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A point circle is the limiting case: as the radius shrinks to zero the circle shrinks to its centre. \((x - h)^{2} + (y - k)^{2} = 0\) is satisfied only when both squares are zero, i.e. only by the single point \((h, k)\).
If the right-hand side were negative, e.g. \((x - 1)^{2} + y^{2} = -4\), no real point satisfies it, because a sum of squares is never negative. We meet this case again in 6.1.2.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A plane cutting a double cone gives a circle, an ellipse, a parabola or a hyperbola; through the vertex it gives a degenerate conic (point, line, pair of lines).
2. Circle: all points at a fixed distance \(r\) (radius) from a fixed point (centre).
3. Standard form: \((x - h)^{2} + (y - k)^{2} = r^{2}\), centre \((h, k)\), radius \(r\).
4. Centre at the origin: \(x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2}\).
5. \(r = 0\) gives a point circle (just the centre).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reading the centre with the wrong signs: \((x + 2)^{2} + (y - 1)^{2} = 25\) has centre \((-2, 1)\), not \((2, -1)\).
2. Taking the radius as the right-hand side: in \((x - 3)^{2} + y^{2} = 16\) the radius is \(\sqrt{16} = 4\), not 16.
3. Forgetting to square the radius when writing the equation: radius 5 gives \(= 25\), not \(= 5\).
